title: Which cocktail means "moist little thing"? | BOOZY WORDS

entries.note: From Arabic [[from:al-kuhl]], 'the kohl' eye makeup, seen as the essence or spirit of a mineral; alchemists used it for fine powders; general drinks sense from the 1600s.
Older than alcohol as a word for the intoxicating part of a liquid; British English says spirits where Americans say [[see:liquor]].
Taken from Latin into Germanic before English existed, via Roman contact; it means vine and is basically the same word as [[same-root:vine]].
One of the words Germanic peoples took from the Romans before English existed, like [[see:wine]].
Another early Roman borrowing into Germanic, like [[see:wine]].
Another early Roman borrowing into Germanic, like [[see:wine]].
Etymologically the same word as [[same-root:wine]], with V and W switching between languages.
Shares its root with [[same-root:wine]] and [[same-root:vine]]: a thing that comes from the vine.
Means sour or sharp wine, related to [[same-root:wine]]; discussed in an earlier episode.
Used only in West Germanic languages; uncertain origin, perhaps a root meaning to drink, [[same-root?:barley]], or [[same-root?:brew]]; ale-drinkers distinguished it as hopped.
Scandinavian languages use variants of it for beer; its root may mean bitter; historically unhopped and English, versus hopped continental [[see:beer]], per Peter Mathias.
Coin-like disc of jewellery; Rob saw one in Oslo inscribed only with [[see:alu]] beside a woman's picture.
Pre-Old Norse word for ale inscribed on a [[see:bracteate]], seemingly jewellery honouring a favourite drink.
English name for certain types of [[see:ale]], fitting the idea that ale's root meant bitter.
Cited for the theory that [[see:beer]] comes from a Romance root meaning to drink.
Slavic word for beer, linked to an Old French word for beer in the Romance theory of [[see:beer]].
[[see:beer]] may come from the same root, a persuasive idea.
[[see:beer]] may come from the same word that gives brew.
Its similarity to [[see:beer]] might just be coincidence.
Swedish generic word for beer (ale), identical to German [[unrelated:Öl (German)]] 'oil' by pure coincidence.
German for oil, coincidentally identical to Swedish [[unrelated:öl (Swedish)]].
Old English could add ale to a word to make a party; this was a post-harvest party.
A bridal party in Old English, the origin of the adjective [[gave:bridal]].
Not a Latin-style adjective but originally a noun, from [[from:bride ale]].
Originally a verb, to drink to excess, from Middle Dutch [[from:busen]], to guzzle; possibly popularised in the US by distiller [[see:Edmund Booz]].
Philadelphia distiller who opened the E.G. Booz distillery in 1840 and made a log-cabin whiskey bottle; his name reputedly helped [[see:booze]] catch on.
Spelled with an E in Ireland and the US, without in Scotland; from Gaelic [[from:uisce beatha]], water of life.
Gaelic term, similar in Scottish Gaelic, that gave [[gave:whiskey]]; many spirits share the name, like [[equivalent:aquavit]] and [[equivalent:eau de vie]].
Scandinavian spirit Rob drank, another spirit named water of life like [[see:uisce beatha]].
Something the Romans had, possibly near-pure alcohol; another water-of-life name like [[see:uisce beatha]].
A fruity French brandy, another spirit named water of life like [[see:uisce beatha]].
Means little water, from Russian [[from:voda]], water, plus a diminutive making it cuter.
Spanish spirit whose name blends [[from:agua]] and [[from:ardiente]], meaning burnt water.
From Dutch [[from:brandewijn]], burnt wine, where burnt means distilled.
Illicit, often unaged corn whiskey, distilled by the light of the moon, from the 18th century; linked to a Wiltshire smuggling legend about [[see:moonraker]].
Alternative to moonshiner; legendary Wiltshire smugglers claimed to be raking a cheese (the moon's reflection) from a pond; unconnected to the James Bond title.
Klondike gold rushers' version of the name of an Alaskan Indigenous people, [[from:Hoochinoo]], whose rum-like liquor was so popular it named unofficial spirits.
The drink's name is thought to come from [[from?:rumbustion]] or [[from?:rumbullion]], words for a racket or chaos, referring to the effects of overdrinking.
Romani-dialect word meaning good, as in [[see:rum kicks]], yet in British English it means odd or bad, making it a [[see:contronym]].
Fancy embroidered trousers, an example of [[see:rum (odd)]] meaning fine.
Good liquor, an example of [[see:rum (odd)]] meaning fine.
The hosts reckon [[see:rum (odd)]] is one, meaning both great and terrible.
From Dutch take on French [[from:genièvre]], juniper, from Latin [[from:juniperus]]; altered by mistaken link with [[see:Geneva]]; invented in the Netherlands, milder London version.
Also Dutch gin: the original, much stronger juniper drink from the Netherlands from which [[see:gin]] developed.
A large cotton-processing machine; its gin is short for [[from:engine]], unrelated to [[unrelated:gin]].
A county where selling liquor isn't allowed, like the one housing the [[see:Jack Daniel's]] distillery.
Distillery in Lynchburg, Tennessee, ironically located in a [[see:dry county]].
Origin disputed, muddied by [[see:H. L. Mencken]]; likeliest from French [[from?:coquetier]], egg cup; other theories: docked horse tails, [[see:cock ale]], a feathered regiment.
Journalist and 'Sage of Baltimore', a troll behind the [[see:Great Bathtub Hoax]] whose 'secret history' spread several [[see:cocktail]] theories.
[[see:H. L. Mencken]]'s 1917 satire convincing readers bathtubs didn't exist in America until the 1850s.
Likeliest source of [[gave?:cocktail]]: [[see:Antoine Amédée Peychaud]] served mixed drinks in egg cups, and a Creole accent could produce the word.
Creole apothecary who created [[see:Peychaud's Bitters]] and served mixed drinks like the [[see:Sazerac]] in an egg cup.
Bitters created by [[see:Antoine Amédée Peychaud]], used in his egg-cup drinks.
Cocktail sometimes said to be the first, served by [[see:Antoine Amédée Peychaud]].
Stale beer and bread fed to fighting roosters, one proposed source of [[see:cocktail]].
Milan bar story: a barman accidentally used sparkling wine instead of gin in a [[from:Negroni]]; Rob prefers it.
Named after Italian aristocrat [[from:Camillo Negroni]], who had gin added to his usual sweet vermouth, Campari and soda.
Not named for containing mimosa flowers but for sharing their yellow colour; called [[equivalent:Buck's Fizz]] in England.
English name for sparkling wine and orange juice, the [[equivalent:mimosa]]; the hosts don't know who the buck is.
Named after the woman's name, though Jess couldn't identify a specific woman.
Probably named after [[from?:Mary I of England]], who had about 280 Protestants burned; leading to a pun on a [[see:crispy Mary]].
Probable namesake of the [[see:Bloody Mary]]; no bloodier than her father, but she had about 280 Protestants burned as heretics.
Joke on the [[see:Bloody Mary]], referencing burnings at the stake and bacon garnishes.
Non-alcoholic [[see:Bloody Mary]]; not the original 'virgin' drink, since virgin [[see:daiquiri]]s came first.
Named after the place in Cuba near Santiago de Cuba where it was invented; virgin versions predate the [[see:Virgin Mary]].
Probably named after a place; the Martinez, California theory is debunked; linked to [[see:Martini & Rossi]] vermouth, but a [[see:Martinez cocktail]] predated it.
Leading vermouth brand proposed as the source of [[see:martini]].
Existed before the [[see:martini]], complicating the timeline of its name.
Brazilian cocktail whose name means a young peasant lady, perhaps for its cheapness.
From Spanish [[from:mojadito]], wet or moist little thing, perhaps from the wet leaves inside.
So named in 1800s cocktail books because it's simple, long made, and avoids frilly juicy ingredients; Jess's favourite.
American usage; British speakers say [[equivalent:spirit]]s instead.
A type of spirit, usually sugary and syrupy, like [[see:Kahlúa]]; pronounced variously.
1930s coffee liqueur name coined by a Spanish sherry family, meaning house of the [[from:Acolhua]] people, Aztec allies.
A Germanized word for [[from:wormwood]], used traditionally to aromatize it, as in [[see:absinthe]].
Contains the same [[see:wormwood]] as [[see:vermouth]], potentially poisonous and hallucinogenic, not in modern form.
A folk etymology of an Old English Germanic compound, perhaps courage-man; the worm story says it protected clothes from moths; also a hawk mite remedy.
From German [[from:schnappen]], to gulp; two Ps in English but one in modern German, which lost one.
An idea that seems great at the time but turns out very bad, as after a few [[see:schnapps]].
Once used for a little bit of alcohol, possibly related to [[same-root?:schnapps]], like [[see:nip]].
Modern equivalent of [[see:snap]] for a small mouthful of alcohol.
Thought of as Scottish for a little whisky; originally a weight, the same that gave [[same-root:dirham]] and [[same-root:drachma]].
Basically acceptable only in Scotch whisky, or a [[see:Scotch egg]].
A boiled egg in sausage meat and breadcrumbs, cheap pub food in Britain but an overpriced gourmet item Jess found in the US.
Moroccan currency from the same weight as [[same-root:dram]].
Old Greek currency from the same weight as [[same-root:dram]].
Chinese drink, the most consumed alcoholic drink in the world; its name means white liquor.
Mandarin for beer: pi imitates [[from:beer]] and jiu means alcohol.
Japanese for beer, from Dutch [[from:bier]], with a final vowel added since Japanese syllables need one except N.
Generic Japanese for booze; what English calls sake is [[equivalent:nihonshu]]; its character, from Chinese, is a pictogram resembling a bottle.
Japanese term for rice wine, what English speakers call [[equivalent:sake]].
One of Jess's favourite terms for drunk; nearly any past participle can mean drunk.
Term for drunk Rob hadn't heard; seems to mean turned to bone.
